headings.title: Introduction to Anatomy and Physiology
headings.content: Anatomy and physiology form the foundation of all medical and nursing sciences. **Anatomy** studies the physical structure and form of body parts, while **physiology** explores how those parts function and work together to sustain life. You cannot truly understand disease without first grasping normal structure and function. Form usually dictates function in the human body; for instance, the delicate, thin walls of the air sacs in the lungs allow oxygen to pass through easily. Gross anatomy looks at large structures visible to the naked eye, whereas microscopic anatomy requires a microscope to see tiny cells and tissues.

headings.title: Levels of Structural Organization
headings.content:
The human body is arranged in a hierarchy of increasing complexity, starting from the smallest chemical building blocks up to the entire organism.

1. **Chemical level**: Atoms combine to form molecules like water, proteins, and DNA.
2. **Cellular level**: Molecules group together to form the basic living units of the body, known as cells.
3. **Tissue level**: Groups of similar cells work together to perform a specific function, such as muscle tissue.
4. **Organ level**: Two or more different tissue types combine to form a recognizable structure with a specific task, like the stomach.
5. **Organ system level**: Multiple organs work in a coordinated fashion to carry out major body activities, such as the digestive system.
6. **Organismal level**: All the organ systems function together to create a complete, living human being.

headings.title: Characteristics of Living Human Organisms
headings.content: Living human beings display distinct life processes that separate them from non-living matter. **Metabolism** encompasses all chemical reactions taking place in the body, combining energy-releasing catabolism with energy-requiring anabolism. **Responsiveness** refers to the ability to sense and react to internal or external changes, such as pulling a hand away from a hot surface. **Movement** happens not just across a room, but also inside the body with blood flow and cellular transport. Other vital traits include growth, cellular differentiation, reproduction, and maintaining boundaries to protect the internal environment.

headings.title: Anatomical Terminology and Body Planes
headings.content:
To prevent confusion when describing patient injuries or surgical sites, healthcare workers use the standard **anatomical position**: standing upright, facing forward, with arms at the sides and palms facing out. 

- **Sagittal plane**: Divides the body vertically into right and left portions.
- **Frontal plane**: Divides the body vertically into anterior (front) and posterior (back) portions.
- **Transverse plane**: Divides the body horizontally into superior (upper) and inferior (lower) portions.

Directional terms like proximal, distal, medial, and lateral give precise location coordinates for physical assessments.

headings.title: Body Cavities and Membranes
headings.content:
The internal organs of the human body are housed within protective spaces called **body cavities**. The two main divisions are the **dorsal body cavity**, which contains the cranial and spinal cavities for the central nervous system, and the **ventral body cavity**, which contains the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities. 

Serous membranes line the ventral cavities and cover the organs inside them. These membranes secrete a slippery lubricating fluid that reduces friction as organs move, such as when the heart beats or the lungs expand during breathing.

headings.title: Homeostasis and Control Systems
headings.content:
Survival depends on maintaining a stable internal environment, a state known as **homeostasis**. Because external conditions change constantly, the body uses feedback loops to make continuous adjustments.

- **Negative feedback loops**: Reverse a directional change to bring variable levels back toward a normal set point, such as shivering when cold or sweating when hot.
- **Positive feedback loops**: Intensify or reinforce the initial stimulus rather than reversing it, such as uterine contractions during childbirth or blood clotting after an injury.

Most physiological control systems in the body rely on negative feedback to keep internal conditions stable.
